Edge cases: get on missing key, put on existing key (update value and move to head), capacity zero, and handling of large objects (memory pressure).

records.text: Bounded per-key ordered task executor. Category: Concurrency. Description: Senior tech screen, Aug 2026: at most 4 tasks run globally, per-key FIFO with no overlap, atomic admission, cancellation, deadline-bounded shutdown; about 25 minutes to hand-code.
key_points: Use a global semaphore (or atomic counter) limited to 4 permits to enforce the global concurrency bound.
Maintain a per‑key FIFO queue; when a task is submitted, enqueue it and attempt to acquire both a global permit and a per‑key lock (e.g., a ReentrantLock per key).
Task admission is atomic: only when both the global permit and the per‑key lock are obtained do you dequeue and run the task; otherwise it stays queued.
Support cancellation by removing the task from its per‑key queue before it starts; deadline‑bounded shutdown iterates over queues, cancels pending tasks, and releases permits.
Complexities: O(1) enqueue/dequeue; overall space O(T) for T pending tasks; thread‑safe via concurrent collections and lock ordering to avoid deadlock.

records.text: Lab machine fleet monitor. Category: System Design. Description: Onsite, Sep 2026: machines poll for payloads; dashboard shows downloading, running, completed, crashed or hung; hang detection vs silent failure, authorized remote reboot, reruns, two-minute inventory refresh.
key_points: Agents on each machine periodically POST their status (polling interval) to a central service; payload includes state enum (DOWNLOADING, RUNNING, COMPLETED, CRASHED, HUNG).
Dashboard queries a time‑series store; use a heartbeat timestamp to differentiate hung (no update beyond threshold) from silent failure (machine offline).
Remote reboot: expose an authenticated RPC endpoint; UI triggers a command that writes a reboot request to a message queue consumed by an agent on the target machine.
Rerun logic: on detection of CRASHED/HUNG, automatically enqueue a new job with same payload; maintain idempotent job IDs to avoid duplicates.
Refresh interval of two minutes is achieved by caching recent statuses and invalidating after 120 s; edge cases include network partitions, clock skew, and partial payload loss.

records.text: High-concurrency incident ticket correlation platform. Category: System Design. Description: Onsite, Aug 2026: interval-based status history, asynchronous idempotent correlation, indexing, freshness markers, reprocessing, audit trail.
key_points: Ingest events into a partitioned log; each interval (e.g., 1 min) writes a compacted snapshot of ticket status history.
Correlation engine runs asynchronously, reading new intervals, applying idempotent correlation rules, and writing results to an indexed store (e.g., Elasticsearch).
Freshness markers (watermarks) indicate the latest processed interval; reprocessing can be triggered by moving the watermark backward.
Audit trail: store raw events plus correlation decisions with timestamps; use append‑only tables for immutability.
Scalability: shard by ticket ID, use back‑pressure queues, and employ eventual consistency; handle edge cases like out‑of‑order arrivals and duplicate events.

records.text: Sizes of 4-connected regions in a binary image, in scan order. Category: Grid / BFS. Description: Sep 2026: component sizes ordered by first-seen cell (Max Area of Island variant).
key_points: Scan the binary matrix row‑wise; when a ‘1’ is encountered that hasn’t been visited, launch a BFS/DFS to compute its 4‑connected component size.
Mark visited cells to avoid recounting; store the size together with the first‑seen cell’s linear index to preserve scan order.
Time complexity O(M · N) for an M×N image; space O(min(M · N, component size)) for the BFS queue/stack.
Edge cases: single‑pixel components, all zeros, all ones, and images with large dimensions that require iterative BFS to avoid stack overflow.
Return the list of sizes sorted by the order of their first discovered cell (i.e., the order of the scan).

records.text: Greedy and top-k beam-search decoding with sentence probability. Category: ML Coding / Heaps. Description: Tech screen, Sep 2026: greedy decoder, then beam search keeping the top-k partial sequences, then explain and correct length bias.
key_points: Greedy decoder: at each step pick the token with highest conditional probability; O(L · V) where L is sequence length and V vocab size.
Beam search: maintain a priority queue of the top‑k partial hypotheses; for each step expand each hypothesis with all possible next tokens, compute cumulative log‑probability, and keep the best k.
Complexity: O(L · k · V) time, O(k · L) space for storing beams; usually V is pruned with a shortlist to reduce cost.
Length bias: beam search tends to favor shorter sequences because probabilities multiply; mitigate by adding length normalization (e.g., divide log‑prob by length^α) or using coverage penalties.
Edge cases: empty vocabulary, ties in scores, handling of EOS token, and ensuring deterministic tie‑breaking for reproducibility.
